column4: The source's dictionary form naʿam (root ن ع م) names camels for the good they bring; this ayah uses al-anʿām and names warmth and benefits, grounding that link in the Qur'an.
The source's herd leaves for pasture and returns; this ayah gives those two daily movements as a beauty for their owners.
The herd's long-distance load carrying appears here, and the ayah closes by calling the Lord compassionate and merciful toward people using the animals.
The section explicitly connects its dictionary form jāʾir to this ayah's crooked ways; the passage moves from livestock to Allah's responsibility for the straight way.
Rain, drinking water, plants, and grazing livestock make this a direct pasture scene, supplying the setting for the section's settled herd.
This ayah directly tells people to eat and pasture their cattle; the preceding 20:53 supplies earth, roads, rain, and vegetation, joining the herd's grazing place to a traversed landscape.
This ayah gives roads through the earth and rain-grown plants; 20:54 completes the scene by naming the cattle that graze there, echoing the section's meeting of path and pasture.
The source's naʿam link is benefit: this ayah names livestock, drink from within them, and other benefits for people.
The section's herd is a working possession; this ayah adds riding livestock and ships, extending the animal's role from pasture and benefit to transport.
The section says a herd belongs to an owner; this ayah says people are made owners of livestock, using mālikūn for that relation.
This ayah says the livestock were subdued for people, a direct counterpart to the section's dictionary description of the tar-coated camel as tamed.
This ayah completes the same livestock passage with further benefits and drink, giving a concrete instance of the good associated with the source's naʿam.
This ayah says livestock were created for people to ride and eat, directly supporting the section's picture of owned, useful animals.
This ayah adds uses, journeys, and carrying loads by livestock and ships; it makes the section's load-bearing animal a shared Qur'anic scene.
This ayah joins a habitable earth, roads, and guidance, paralleling the section's move from a settled pasture to the request to be led on a path.
This ayah names livestock among the paired things made for riding, a direct scene of animals placed in human service.
The ayah describes settling on the backs of subdued animals and remembering the Lord; it joins the section's tamed mount to its language of divine ownership.
The riding passage ends by returning to the Lord; this ayah's contribution is to place the animal journey under the same Lord named as owner in the section.
This ayah explicitly brings out the earth's water and pasture, matching the section's valued grazing ground.
This ayah names pasture as provision for people and their livestock, making explicit who benefits from the grazing land in the section.
The ayah uses ḍāllan and then says God guided; it gives the section's lost-animal image a precise Qur'anic movement from being lost to receiving guidance, while leaving their contexts distinct.
This ayah gathers wild beasts immediately after the neglected camels of 81:4, completing the section's striking contrast between abandoned domestic animals and wild herds.
The she-camel is explicitly God's sign and is left to graze on God's land; this closely joins animal ownership, grazing, and a boundary against harming the animal.
Like 7:73, this ayah names God's she-camel and permits her to graze on God's land, making divine ownership and pasture explicit together.
Moses finds women holding back their flock until the shepherds water theirs; this gives the section's herd a human keeper and a shared watering scene.
Moses waters the women's flock after meeting them in 28:23; this ayah supplies the act of care that completes that shepherd-and-herd scene.
A flock of sheep wanders into a field and damages its crop; the ayah places a straying herd under human judgment, a close counterpart to the section's escaped camel.

The ayah asks whether one who guides to truth is more worthy to be followed; it states directly the leader-and-follower relation that the section draws from its dictionary forms for the herd's fore-animal and guide.
Abraham asks his father to follow him because he will guide him to a straight path; this turns the section's animal guide and following herd into an explicit human-guidance scene.
This ayah calls prophets leaders who guide by God's command, a direct parallel to the section's dictionary form for the animal that goes ahead and guides the rest.
This ayah likewise describes leaders who guide by God's command; it adds patience and certainty as the qualities behind sound leadership.
Every people is called with its imam; the ayah makes the section's leading animal and following herd a social image of followers gathered with a leader.
The source's dictionary form hawādī names the necks or leading band of horses; this ayah names horses and donkeys as riding animals, though it does not itself describe them leading a herd.
This ayah draws milk from cattle as a pure drink, a concrete benefit that fits the section's explanation of livestock as bringing good.
The source's dictionary form calls the leading bee the malīk al-naḥl; this ayah presents bees as receiving direction from their Lord, giving the bee-leader gloss a divine-guidance counterpart.
The bee is told to follow its Lord's made-easy paths; this is a specific parallel to the section's bee leader and to the image of a follower taking a guided route.
This ayah describes creatures moving on bellies, two legs, or four; it gives a Qur'anic counterpart to the section's dictionary detail that a riding animal is carried by its legs.
This ayah calls land creatures and birds communities and says they will be gathered to their Lord; it gives the section's wild herds a Qur'anic frame as animal communities.
The section's stray camel has no known human owner in a desolate place; this ayah says every creature's provision and settled place are known to God, extending care beyond visible ownership.
The ayah says many creatures do not carry their own provision and that God provides for them; it offers a specific counterpart to the camel stranded without a known owner.
Moses describes using his staff to tend his sheep; this adds a herdsman's practical care to the section's owned and guided flock.
Abraham says that without his Lord's guidance he would be among the astray; this shares the section's request for guidance and makes dependence on a guide explicit.
This ayah joins praise (ḥamd) to God's ownership of what is in the heavens and earth; it frames the source's liked pasture and humanly ownerless camel within divine ownership.
The fleeing donkeys give the section's wild-donkey herd a direct animal scene, while their flight from a lion reverses the calm movement of a herd following its guide.
This ayah identifies the donkeys of 74:50 as fleeing from a lion; that detail completes the wild-herd image with the danger they flee.
This ayah names sacrificial camels among God's symbols and says they have been subjected for people, joining the camel image to divine ownership and service.
The she-camel has a designated turn to drink, with a turn for the people; this gives a concrete water boundary around an animal that grazes on land.
The she-camel is sent as a trial and people are told to watch; this makes the camel a possession and sign under divine authority.
The water is divided between the people and the she-camel; the ayah adds an explicit limit on human use of an animal's shared pasture environment.
The people are warned about God's she-camel and her drink; this links the animal's ownership to a protected share of water.
This ayah distinguishes livestock used for carrying from other kinds and permits eating from them; it gives the section's useful herd a more explicit division of work and food.
This ayah brings forth pasture; 87:5 immediately shows it becoming dark debris, extending the section's valued grazing ground into a cycle of change.
The people hamstring the she-camel after being warned to leave her; this is the reversal of the section's owned camel being kept and recognized.
The people hamstring the protected she-camel of 11:64, turning the granted grazing boundary into its violation.
After the she-camel's protected drinking turn, the people hamstring her; the animal's allotted place is violently broken.
The people call their companion, who hamstrings the she-camel; the act reverses the care and restraint around a herd animal.
The people deny the warning and hamstring the she-camel, a direct reversal of leaving a known animal in safety.
The ayah says Pharaoh led his people astray and did not guide them; it reverses the section's good fore-animal who leads a herd along a way.
This ayah calls rulers leaders to the Fire; it is the opposite of the section's guide whose followers are led toward the straight path.
People blame their chiefs for leading them astray; it gives the follower's consequence when the section's guide-and-herd relation fails.
The pasture of 87:4 becomes dark debris in this ayah; the scene reverses the section's favored grazing place by showing its later disappearance.
The pregnant camels left unattended reverse the section's cared-for, owned herd and its lost camel; here even valuable camels are neglected.
This ayah compares heedless people to livestock and says they are more astray; it reverses the section's claim that an animal can lose its way while still recognizing its herd and owner.
This ayah also calls people like livestock, even more astray in the way; its explicit reversal sharpens the section's distinction between an animal and a human who will not follow guidance.
The command not to harm the she-camel sets a boundary around the animal placed in human care, reversing the runaway camel's loss from its owner.
The cow here has not been yoked to plow or water a field; it is a boundary case against the section's tamed camel used for work and carrying.
The source's dictionary entry says a lost camel is called ḍālla whether male or female; this ayah shows a contrasting rule that divides livestock by sex.
This ayah sorts sheep and goats into male-female pairs; against the source's gender-neutral dictionary form for a lost camel, it shows another Qur'anic way of classifying herds.
This ayah asks about male and female camels and cattle; it makes a specific contrast with the source's statement that either sex can be a ḍālla.
The source's dictionary form wasm is a mark by which a camel is recognized; this ayah names garlanded sacrificial animals, whose visible marker signals sacred status rather than a human owner.
This ayah calls the garlands on sacrificial animals signs; like the source's mark on a camel, they identify an animal, but here the status is sacred protection.

This ayah rejects customary categories of animals deliberately released from ordinary use; it contrasts an intentionally designated free animal with the section's camel that escapes and loses its known owner.
After 22:36's sacrificed camels, this ayah says their meat and blood do not reach God but piety does; it limits what the camel offering means in relation to its divine owner.
The parable counts one man's ninety-nine ewes against another's single ewe and depicts an oppressive claim to another's flock; it complicates the section's simple relation between herd and owner.
